title: Searching and Extracting Data from Files

sections.title: Mission · Search, Filter, and Transform Text
paragraphs: Linux becomes powerful when small commands work together. You can display, search, filter, sort, extract, and count data, then redirect output or pipe it into another command.
bullets: grep, less, cat, head, tail, sort, cut, and wc
sections.callout: BUILD SMALL COMMANDS INTO A DATA-PROCESSING PIPELINE

sections.title: Standard Input, Output, and Error
paragraphs: Command-line programs commonly use three data streams: STDIN is standard input, STDOUT is normal output, and STDERR is error output. Understanding these streams explains pipes and redirection.

sections.title: cat
paragraphs: cat displays file contents. cat notes.txt prints the file directly. It can also combine data, but basic recognition begins with showing a file.

sections.title: less
paragraphs: less lets you view text interactively, especially when a file is too long for one screen. less hugefile.txt lets you move through content instead of dumping it all at once.

sections.title: Exam Trap · cat vs. less
sections.callout: HUGE LOG FILE? LESS IS USUALLY MORE CONVENIENT

sections.title: head
paragraphs: head displays the beginning of a file or input. head logfile.txt is useful when you only want the first portion.

sections.title: tail
paragraphs: tail displays the end of a file or input. Logs are commonly examined from the end because the newest entries are often there.

sections.title: head vs. tail
sections.callout: HEAD IS ON TOP · TAIL IS AT THE END

sections.title: grep
paragraphs: grep searches text for matching patterns. grep error logfile.txt finds lines in logfile.txt containing error. It is one of the most important Linux text-processing commands.

sections.title: sort
paragraphs: sort arranges lines of text. sort names.txt places lines in order; exact ordering can depend on options and environment.

sections.title: cut
paragraphs: cut extracts portions or fields from lines. It is useful when data has consistent fields or delimiters, such as extracting one field from jsmith:HelpDesk, maria:IT, and dsmith:Users.

sections.title: wc
paragraphs: wc means word count. It can count lines, words, and bytes or characters depending on its options. A common scenario is counting lines.

sections.title: Pipes
paragraphs: The pipe operator | sends one command's output into another command's input. In cat logfile.txt | grep error, cat outputs the file and grep searches that output.
sections.callout: | = TAKE THIS OUTPUT AND GIVE IT TO THE NEXT COMMAND

sections.title: Why Pipes Are Powerful
paragraphs: Linux commands often perform focused tasks, and pipes combine them. cat users.txt | sort reads then sorts. grep error logfile.txt | wc -l finds matching lines and then counts them.

sections.title: Output Redirection
paragraphs: > redirects standard output into a file. echo GSA > academy.txt writes GSA to academy.txt instead of only displaying it.

sections.title: Overwrite Warning
paragraphs: A single > normally replaces the destination file's existing contents. If academy.txt already contains data, echo GSA > academy.txt can overwrite it.

sections.title: Append Redirection
paragraphs: >> appends output to the end of a file. echo Linux >> academy.txt keeps existing content and adds the new line.

sections.title: Input Redirection
paragraphs: < redirects input from a file into a command. For Linux Essentials, recognize the general direction of I/O redirection.

sections.title: Regular Expressions
paragraphs: A regular expression, or regex, describes a text pattern. This objective requires recognition of ., [ ], *, and ?. Regex is not the same as shell globbing: similar symbols can behave differently depending on the interpreter.
sections.callout: CONTEXT DETERMINES WHETHER THE SHELL OR REGEX ENGINE INTERPRETS THE SYMBOL

sections.title: Regex Dot · .
paragraphs: In a regular-expression context, . matches a single character. c.t can match cat or cut.

sections.title: Character Classes · [ ]
paragraphs: Square brackets specify a set of characters. [abc] matches one character that is a, b, or c. gr[ae]y can match gray or grey.

sections.title: Regex *
paragraphs: In basic regular expressions, * means the preceding element can occur zero or more times. ab* can match an a followed by zero or more b characters.

sections.title: Major Exam Trap · Glob * vs. Regex *
paragraphs: In the shell glob *.txt, * broadly matches filename characters. In the basic regex ab*, * repeats the preceding element zero or more times. The symbol is the same, but the context and interpretation differ.

sections.title: Question Mark Awareness
paragraphs: The official objective includes ? among basic regular-expression symbols to recognize. Do not assume it always means the same thing: in shell globbing, ? matches one filename character; regular-expression behavior depends on the regex flavor and context.
sections.callout: THE EXAM TARGET IS BASIC PATTERN RECOGNITION, NOT ADVANCED REGEX ENGINEERING

sections.title: Combining grep with Patterns
paragraphs: grep becomes especially powerful with regex patterns. grep 'c.t' words.txt can find matching text where the dot represents one character.

sections.title: GSA Scenario Recognition
bullets: Display an entire short text file → cat
Interactively browse a long text file → less
Search lines for matching text → grep
Send one command's output to another → |
Write output to a file, replacing content → >
Add output to the end of a file → >>
Take command input from a file → <
